kill_fact: The adverse case is mislabelled by roughly a full commodity cycle: sop_bear says it assumes 'the 62% benchmark sustained near $80 per tonne', but the arithmetic it actually applies is a $14/t realised-price fall ($4.6B on 330 Mt). At the record's own realisation ratio - Vale's 2Q26 release (2026-07-31) reports a realised fines price of $95.0/t against a $108.27 Q2 62% Fe average, i.e. 87.7% - a $14/t realised fall corresponds to a benchmark of about $92, which is essentially the $94.45 the index printed on 2026-08-11. So $9.50 is not a downside scenario at all; it is the value of the record's own schedule at TODAY'S iron ore price. A genuine $80/t sustained deck implies realised ~$70.2/t, a $24.8/t fall, or ~$8.2B of EBITDA on 330 Mt - cutting iron-ore-and-pellets EBITDA from $7.6B to ~$4.0B and, on the record's own 5.5x/6.5x multiples, -$1.0B corporate and $18.0B expanded net debt, an equity value of $23.2B, or $5.43 per share on 4.266B diluted shares (FMP 2Q26). The record therefore carries no modelled adverse case, and the risk_reward statement that there is 'roughly four times as much room below to the adverse case as above to fair value' understates the true asymmetry rather than overstating it. This corrects the number in the direction of the record's own conclusion, so the finding - poor risk/reward at the quoted price - survives the attack.
corrections: (1) MATERIAL, bear_px: $9.50 -> $5.50. sop_bear's stated $80/t benchmark and its applied $14/t realised price fall are inconsistent by roughly $11/t of realised price, about $3.6B of annualised EBITDA. Re-derived on the record's own schedule (iron ore EBITDA $4.0B at 5.5x = $22.0B; base metals $3.8B at 6.5x = $24.7B; corporate -$1.0B at 5.5x = -$5.5B; EV $41.2B less $18.0B expanded net debt = $23.2B equity / 4.266B shares) gives $5.43; published at $5.50. Two partial offsets are acknowledged and deliberately not netted, because they are judgement rather than arithmetic: trough earnings would plausibly capitalise above the 5.5x the record chose, and a $23B market value would sit near the ~$26B the 2023 Manara transaction implied for the base-metals arm alone. (2) MINOR, prose only, no level moves: the bear thesis states 'roughly a third' of the $16.677B expanded net debt is the reparation obligation. Vale's 2Q26 filing shows Brumadinho provisions of $1,774M plus Samarco provisions of $2,097M = $3,871M, or 23% - net debt is $13,173M. The CFO's non-refinanceable point stands; the weight of it is about a third smaller than claimed. (3) MINOR, prose only: sop_bear's aside that removing the currency offset 'drops the arithmetic to roughly $8.00-$8.50' does not reconcile - removing the stated $0.6B of FX relief from the record's own uncorrected schedule gives $9.30, not $8.00-$8.50. (4) NOTE, not a correction: valuation.live_price of $14.875 is stale as of 2026-08-04; VALE closed at $14.265 on 2026-08-11, down 4.2% on the day. (5) NOTE for the Director, unmodelled by the bear leg: the cyclical-peak risk in this name is currently in COPPER, not iron ore. The 62% Fe index at $94.45 sits at the bottom of its 52-week $93.66-$111.42 range, so the valuation is not passing on peak iron ore. But Vale realised $14,062/t of copper in 2Q26, +57% y/y, and COMEX copper at $6.64/lb on 2026-08-11 is within 1.3% of its 52-week high and 13% above its 200-day average of $5.86. sop_bear's $3.8B base-metals EBITDA is nominally struck at '$8,000 per tonne' copper, but on ~400kt of annual copper sales a $6,000/t price fall is about $2.4B against a current base-metals run rate near $5.5B (2Q26 pro forma EBITDA $4.066B annualised, less the $11.6B iron ore run rate, plus $1.0B corporate), implying about $3.1B rather than $3.8B. That residual generosity is not carried into the correction above, and it is the direction in which the bear leg is still too kind.
